claims.text: In-situ ML-driven feedback during LPBF of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce compositional segregation relative to fixed-parameter LPBF.
In-situ ML-driven feedback during LPBF of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce residual thermal stresses relative to fixed-parameter LPBF.
In-situ ML-driven feedback during LPBF of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce defect formation relative to fixed-parameter LPBF.
Standard LPBF of AlCrFeNiSi typically produces compositional segregation, high residual stress, and defects.
Laser power and scan speed are key LPBF process parameters affecting HEA processability and defect formation.
The proposed controller will dynamically adjust laser power, scan speed, and localized preheating from real-time thermal-imaging data.
Dynamic control of laser parameters will modify the local melt-pool thermal profile and cooling rate.
Modification of the melt-pool thermal profile and cooling rate will produce a more uniform microstructure with less segregation.
Modification of the melt-pool thermal profile and cooling rate will produce a more balanced residual-stress distribution.
Optimizing heat input and cooling dynamics will mitigate rapid cooling and thermal gradients.
Reduced cooling rates and thermal gradients will lower the driving forces for segregation, residual-stress buildup, and defects such as hot cracks.
ML-controlled LPBF will reduce residual stress by more than 20% relative to conventional processing.
A more homogeneous microstructure will enhance the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi.
The hypothesis is limited to LPBF of cobalt-free HEAs under comparable thermal, geometric, and powder-feedstock conditions and may not transfer to other AM methods or radically different alloys.
The magnitude and geometric uniformity of improvement depend on sensor accuracy, ML algorithm efficacy, and local process variation.

A controlled comparison using identical powder, geometry, and environment can test fixed-parameter LPBF against ML-controlled LPBF using residual-stress, SEM/EDS, tensile, and fracture-toughness measurements.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant residual-stress reduction near or above 20%, together with no improvement in homogeneity or mechanical properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
